toc.title: Trauma is the response, not the event
The events that can lead to trauma

sections.title: Path one: an acute life threat reaction
Path two: a chronic disruption of connectedness

blocks.p: So how does all of this connect to trauma? From the Polyvagal Theory, trauma is being stuck in a defensive state: stuck in flight or fight, stuck in shutdown, stuck in freeze. Being stuck in those states is trauma. That's why my podcast is called Stuck Not Broken.
Dr. Porges said it well on the podcast: "The warmest home for the polyvagal theory... is in trauma." ([Episode 15](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/a3c6a54a-11a7-4f2f-9d74-db287c774d08))

blocks.h: Trauma is the response, not the event

blocks.p: Trauma is the response to the event, not the event itself. That's not the way we typically think. But from the Polyvagal Theory, trauma is not the car crash. Trauma is the state we're left in after the car crash.

Let's say we're on a bus together, and the bus crashes. We're in the exact same situation, and we both walk away from it. One of us might be able to take a deep breath and say, "Oh my gosh, that was unbelievable. Are you okay?" And we're mostly okay.

The other person may have gone into freeze, where they're mobilized but also forced to immobilize. They're locked in more of a paralysis, or at least that energy is in their system. They walk off that bus still in that freeze state, and they're not able to self-regulate. They're not able to check in with the other person. They're not able to breathe and calm down.

So the same event can lead to different responses. That's why we say the trauma is not the event, it's the response to the event. Of course, some events are more likely to leave you in a traumatized state, absolutely. But it's the response.

blocks.h: The events that can lead to trauma

blocks.p: There are different types of events that can lead to trauma.

One-time events. A car accident, an injury, even childhood falls, violent attacks, and assaults, especially in childhood and especially when they're unexpected. Unexpected matters. You can box with somebody: you go into a ring, you expect to be hit, you expect to be beaten up. That's not traumatic in the same way that being assaulted and physically beaten up would be.

Ongoing, relentless stress. The neighborhood you live in, a life-threatening illness, being bullied, domestic violence, child neglect, abuse. These are ongoing and repeated, so they're relentless. There's no way to run away, and maybe no way to fight them off. This could leave someone in a traumatized state, even a shutdown or a freeze state, but probably one of the defensive states. Bullying is something I don't think we take seriously, but from my experience working with kids, it really affects them.

Commonly overlooked causes. Surgery is one. If you go into surgery while you're really in a flight or fight state, and then you're forced to immobilize, that could leave you in a traumatized state. Others are the sudden death of somebody close, the breakup of a significant relationship, humiliation, and a deeply disappointing experience, especially if someone's being deliberately cruel.

We tend to overlook these, and they can be some level of trauma in and of themselves. But I'd also look at them as possibly the last straw. Maybe there's something you've gone through, or are going through, and then there's the death of somebody close, and now you really do exist in a traumatized state.

Back then, the kids I worked with had very traumatic lives. What's interesting is that if I asked them, "When did things really change for you?" a lot of times they'd say, "When I lost my parent." When their safety person was not in their life anymore. When a parent left them, or a grandparent died. That's what I heard a lot: my grandparent died. Even though they'd been through all kinds of horrifying stuff, the death of that one person close to them was the moment things really changed, and that's what they'd tell me.

To make this a little more convoluted, those events can take two different paths to trauma: an acute life threat reaction, or a chronic disruption of connectedness. The one-time events tend to lead to the first. The ongoing, relentless stress is probably more the second. What it looks like will be different from person to person.

blocks.h3: Path one: an acute life threat reaction

blocks.p: Examples here would be a car crash, a school shooting, a terrorist attack, an assault, war. I'd say this is more likely to leave someone in a freeze state, where they were immobilized while highly charged, while in flight or fight. And I'd relate this path to PTSD, post-traumatic stress disorder.

In an acute life threat reaction, the nervous system is frozen. That's where the word freeze really applies. It's frozen in the moment of survival. The impulse to run away or fight wasn't able to complete, because there was also immobility. That leaves someone with a frozen flavor of flight and fight, plus shutdown: freeze.
Later on, aspects of the event can trigger that state: scents, sights, locations, people. That can trigger a flashback, or bring that flight and fight energy back to the surface.
Here's an example from an article called Twenty Years Later at Columbine:

q: "Martin did not sustain physical injuries during Columbine, so initially she didn't realize how deeply set her trauma was. Plus, she learned she was a changed person after a fire alarm went off in class during her freshman year of college. She says, 'I started crying and I didn't even understand why I was crying.' She later realized that the fire alarm was a trigger related to Columbine. She had been locked in a tiny room with 60 other students hiding that day, and the fire alarm was going off the entire time."

blocks.p: So you have someone with a sensory experience, the fire alarm, that's connected to the experience of being immobile while having the impulse to run or fight.

Someone on this path of trauma can have a fulfilling life. They can have relationships, they can meet their goals. It's possible. But they might avoid aspects of the event: the people involved, obviously, the places, sensory stimuli like the fire alarm. Because those aspects of the event will trigger that state to come back.

blocks.h3: Path two: a chronic disruption of connectedness

blocks.p: Examples here would be neglect, ongoing abuse, divorce, domestic violence. I think this path could leave someone stuck in any of the states: flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze.

I'd say this is more closely related to complex post-traumatic stress disorder, CPTSD, because there's an element of disconnection: having your attachment, your safe connections, severed repeatedly. So there are the traumatic incidents someone goes through, plus the disconnections from a safe other. That adds another layer to the trauma.

This person exists in a chronic state of defense. They can't really avoid aspects of the event the way someone with an acute life threat reaction might be able to. That flavor is always in their system.

Kids especially are susceptible to this. They have a biological reliance on the adults in their life, and that puts them at a higher risk of this path of trauma. Attachment has a lot to do with it: the impulse to connect. That's a necessity of being a child. It's a guiding biological impulse within every single one of us, to attach to the people in our life. Hopefully they're safe, hopefully they're predictable, hopefully there's some structure, and a safe, healthy, loving attachment.

That attachment is absolutely essential for other life milestones. If a healthy attachment isn't set, then milestones like making friends and finding relationships become a lot more challenging. People who have been through a chronic disruption of connectedness can have a lot of difficulty identifying and maintaining safe and trusting relationships. Identifying safe people can be a significant challenge for them.

Ideally, we'd exist in a safe and social state all the time. That's not realistic. None of us do that. So each of us probably has what we call a home away from home: the defensive state you're in more often than not.
So reflect for yourself. What's your home away from home? Flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze? What state do you spend more time in than not?
For me, it's easily shutdown. Probably my whole life, I've had more of a shutdown flavor in my system than anything else. That's not bad. It just is what it is.

My hope is that you see this, and instead of seeing each other as people who are always in a fully conscious state, who can make clear-headed choices and weigh pros and cons, you see that we are people who exist in these states, and then make decisions, implement policies, go to work, and do our work.

First and foremost, we are organisms, mammals, that exist with these states. Then we interact with each other, come to work, and do our therapeutic modalities, whatever it is. This is what we bring to work. This is what we bring to our relationships and our friendships. Seeing that can help us gain some empathy for each other.
